topics.name: Satellites can be listened to, jammed and hacked
topics.then: The book shows that satellite links were left open (an enthusiast watching NATO spy pictures in 2002) and that Russia attacked the Viasat KA-SAT network on the first day of the Ukraine invasion, while Starlink held up.
topics.now: The US and EU publicly blamed Russia for the KA-SAT attack in May 2022, and US agencies issued a warning to satellite network providers. Russia's jamming of Starlink over Ukraine is a continuing, documented contest, tracked each year by the Secure World Foundation.
topics.ai: AI cuts both ways: it helps defenders spot strange traffic on modems and ground stations, and it speeds up the search for bugs in open-source flight software.
topics.we_do: We counted which open-source space software projects publish a list of what is inside them (a software bill of materials). One of nine did. We are now building that list for NASA's core flight software ourselves.
topics.opportunity: Small companies can sell software inventories, key management and ground-station hardening to small satellite operators. The US warning gives buyers a ready checklist.

topics.name: The view from above: climate, El Niño and the sunshade idea
topics.then: The book uses satellite tracking of El Niño and the long climate record to argue that space gives us the planet's history, then floats a sunshade at the L1 point between Earth and Sun to block a little sunlight.
topics.now: NOAA issued an El Niño Advisory on 8 Oct 2026. The sunshade has grown from one-off papers into a small field: a 2025 preliminary design of a precursor mission and the first international sunshade workshop in May 2026. None has flown.
topics.ai: AI makes the satellite archives searchable by people who are not climate scientists. For a sunshade, the hard part is steering a swarm of thin sails, which is a simulation and control problem.
topics.we_do: In the episode we ask the question nobody in the papers answers well: if someone can dim the Sun, who decides, and who can switch it off?
topics.opportunity: Earth-observation analytics sold to insurers, farmers and utilities. A strong El Niño year is when buyers look for better forecasts.

topics.name: Space weather: Carrington, Quebec and the next big storm
topics.then: The 1859 Carrington storm and the 1989 Quebec blackout show that a solar storm can take down a power grid, and could again.
topics.now: How big Carrington was is now given as a range, not one number (USGS, 2024). The May 2024 storm reached G5, the top of NOAA's scale. NOAA's new solar-wind satellite, SOLAR-1 (launched as SWFO-L1 on 24 Sep 2025), reached its L1 orbit in January 2026.
topics.ai: AI models are being trained to predict solar eruptions earlier, but warning time is still set by physics: we see the eruption, then measure the solar wind at L1, roughly 15 to 60 minutes before it reaches Earth.
topics.we_do: Our TechLeap entry measures air density in low orbit, which is exactly what a solar storm changes. We tie the two together without claiming more than the instrument can show.
topics.opportunity: Drag and storm-alert data for satellite operators, and outage planning for companies on the ground.

sources.label: USGS, On the uncertain intensity estimate of the 1859 Carrington storm (2024)
NOAA NESDIS, SOLAR-1 (ex SWFO-L1) press kit

topics.name: Impacts and planetary defense
topics.then: Chicxulub, Tunguska and Chelyabinsk show the hazard. Congress ordered a survey in 2005, and surveys like Catalina are the response.
topics.now: The 2005 law's goal (find 90% of near-Earth objects 140 m and larger by 2020) was missed. Catalina still leads on spotting small asteroids hours before they hit: 2026 RW1 was seen about six hours before it fell into the Indian Ocean in September 2026. A 2024 study traced the dinosaur-killer to a carbon-rich asteroid from beyond Jupiter.
topics.ai: Software is the bottleneck, not telescopes: a tracking algorithm run on old archive images found about 27,500 new asteroid candidates in 2024. That was clever search code, not AI.
topics.we_do: We time an episode to ESA's Hera arriving at the asteroid DART hit. The number we want to build: how many impacts were caught before they happened, year by year.
topics.opportunity: Orbit software and follow-up observing on public telescope archives. The missed 90% goal is a documented, unmet mandate.
